newsitem.title: USA: U.S. to continue to press China on human rights.
newsitem.headline: U.S. to continue to press China on human rights.

text.p: The Clinton administration will continue to press China on human rights issues while pursuing dialogue on a range of other interests, U.S. National Security Adviser Anthony Lake said on Sunday.

Following a meeting between President Bill Clinton and Chinese President Jiang Zemin in Manila and an announcement that they would exchange state visits within the next two years, Lake said the administration still wanted China to improve its human rights record, which he called "not very good."
Human rights activists had objected to the meeting in Manila because of alleged rights abuses by Beijing.

"We will continue to press them on it. We will continue to pursue our interests in human rights like our interests in opening the Chinese market and getting good Chinese performance on non-proliferation issues," Lake said on NBC television's "Meet the Press."
He said the Clinton administration had successfully put human rights on the agenda with Beijing in its first year by linking them to free trade issues.
"Now we think the best way to pursue it is to have this dialogue with the Chinese," he said.
Retiring Sen. Sam Nunn, speaking on the same show, said the planned summits were a good idea.

"Isolation of China and basically having unilateral sanctions against China are not only not working but they are counterproductive to human rights in China," said the Georgian, who is the top Democrat on the Senate Armed Services Committee.

Senate Minority Leader Tom Daschle of South Dakota reinforced the Democrats' shift away from linking trade and human rights, saying said he would favour giving China permanent trade preferences as a "most favoured nation" to build a better relationship with Beijing.
"I favour making it permanent," Daschle said on Fox television's "Fox News Sunday."
Addressing concerns that North Korea might have suspended its commitment to stop developing nuclear weapons, Lake said he was confident that its nuclear programme remained frozen.
"They have not said that as a matter of policy they have suspended it. We hope that they will not," he said.
"The North Korean nuclear programme is frozen under international supervision, and we think that it can be totally stood down," he added.
